subject: bicycle
pitch: A vintage Dutch city bicycle in mint green. Tall upright handlebars with cream grips and a silver bell, a brown leather saddle with springs, chrome mudguards, a chain guard, a wicker basket on the front filled with sunflowers and a baguette, and whitewall tyres.
reasoning:
I'm planning to build a vintage Dutch city bicycle using the three.js agentic-3js-builder SDK, working with the documented primitives like joints, chains, sweeps, parts, and surfaces since I don't have full API documentation beyond what's referenced.

Since a bicycle isn't a creature, I'm thinking about using joints mainly for the wheel hubs to enable rotation, while relying on plain three.js geometry attached to those joints for the actual wheel meshes. I need to be careful about exact function signatures for things like joint parenting, part placement, and the rod/stick/capsule geometry helpers since their usage is somewhat ambiguous from the reference.

For the frame tubes, I'm settling on using sweep with a simple two-point polyline path and a radius, since that's a documented and reliable way to create tube geometry between points rather than guessing at rod or capsule signatures.

Now I'm sketching out the rig: a root "frame" joint, a steering joint at the head tube for the handlebars and front wheel assembly, and hub joints for front/rear wheels that spin around their axle axis. I'm working out rough real-world dimensions — 28" wheels (radius ~0.33m), bottom bracket height ~0.30m, and a wheelbase of roughly 1.05m with front and rear hubs placed symmetrically along the +Z/-Z axis since the bike faces +Z.

I'm laying out the diamond-style frame geometry: bottom bracket, seat tube, head tube, top tube, and seat positions with specific coordinates, plus chainstays and seat stays connecting to the rear hub, with dropouts offset slightly in x for left/right symmetry.

For the wheels I'm setting up a rotated torus geometry so its axis runs along x instead of z, then layering a dark tyre torus with a thinner whitewall ring offset for that classic sidewall look.

Checking the math, the cream torus protrudes slightly past the tyre surface, which reads correctly as a whitewall band. I'm adding a thin silver torus for the rim and planning spokes as small cylinders rotated radially around each wheel, roughly 16 per wheel for a total of 32 extra parts.

Still working out spoke and mudguard placement...

Working out the rotation math...

I'm settling on a thetaStart near π/2-1.9 with thetaLength around 3.8 to span the fender arc, using an outer radius of about 0.40 above the wheel hub. I'm weighing whether to use one open-ended cylinder band or two nested ones for a cleaner fender shell, but deciding a single outward-facing band is sufficient since it's only viewed from outside — this is getting more complex than it needs to be, though.

Now I'm checking whether the fender's width and position at x=0 would collide with the fork blades, since the fork runs near the top of the wheel where the fender sits, so I need to verify the fork path doesn't pass through the fender geometry.

Since fenders and forks naturally overlap near the crown on real bikes, I'll accept that intersection and move on to simpler parts: a chain guard box near the BB and a cylindrical chainring on the drivetrain side, keeping colors dark for the guard and silver for the ring.

Then I'm sketching the chain as two thin dark sweeps connecting the chainring to the rear sprocket, and defining the handlebars as an upright "opafiets" style curve with a stem rising from the head tube and a swept chrome tube forming the bar shape through catmull-rom points.

I'm adding cream grip cylinders swept along short segments at each bar end, pointing backward from the curved tips.

Now I'm placing a silver bell hemisphere on the handlebar's right side near the center, and shaping the saddle as a flattened, scaled sphere in brown leather sitting atop the seatpost, with stacked small tori forming a stylized coil spring underneath.

Then I'm sweeping the seatpost from the seat tube up to the saddle base, and designing a wicker front basket as a tapered box or frustum shape mounted above the front wheel near the handlebars.

I'll stylize the sunflowers with flat yellow discs and brown centers on bent green stems, using a torus for the petal ring to keep things simple, with four flowers positioned across the basket. For the baguette, I'll use a capsule shape lying diagonally in the basket with a few darker boxes as score marks.

I'm defining the color palette: mint green frame, cream grips, silver chrome, dark tyres, brown leather seat, tan basket and baguette, yellow sunflowers, and gold springs. Now I'm building the wheel geometry function with tyre, whitewall, rim, hub, and spoke tori/cylinders arranged symmetrically around each axle.

Writing wheel geometry...

Adding hub and rim geometry, then realizing the solid tyre torus will hide the spokes and rim entirely—I need to rethink the tyre shape so the spokes remain visible from the side, perhaps by hollowing it out or exposing a gap.

I'll adjust the whitewall ring proportions so it sits as a side bulge against the tyre rather than overlapping awkwardly, widening the tyre itself to 0.09 and spreading the wheels to match. For the fork and frame, I'm positioning the blades as swept tubes running from the crown down to the front dropouts, and similarly building chainstays and seatstays as swept tube pairs connecting the bottom bracket and seat tube to the rear hub.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: a root frame joint, a front wheel joint parented to it, and a steer joint at the head tube top for the fork and handlebar. I want to make sure sweep calls explicitly specify their bone when possible, since that should take priority over automatic bone assignment based on proximity.

Naming the joints as "frame", "wheelF", "wheelR", "steer", and considering a "saddle" joint, though chains/roles aren't needed since the frame is rigid. I'm debating whether to add a brass headlamp near the fork crown but worry it'll overlap with the basket, so I may skip it to keep things simple.

Working out the drivetrain geometry: positioning the chainring and crank arms at the bottom bracket offset slightly on the x-axis, with the chain running to a rear sprocket aligned near the rear hub. I'm sketching crank arm sweeps from the BB outward to pedal positions, keeping it simple with basic shapes for the pedals.

For the chain guard, I'm considering using a curved band geometry similar to the fenders -- a cylindrical arc oriented around the bottom bracket axis to cover the top of the chainring, reusing the band-generation function with a narrower width and appropriate radius.

For the front wheel fender, I'm working out the arc angles so the band wraps from front-bottom around to back-bottom, keeping the curve positioned below the hub center.

For the rear fender I'll mirror that same band logic, then fine-tune the band dimensions (width, radial segments, chrome color) and decide the bell's placement as a small dome on the right handlebar, before sketching basket details like sunflower stems rising from the basket interior.

Now I'm working out the sunflower heads: disk-shaped centers with torus petals facing outward, mounted on slightly curved green stems rising from the basket, with four flowers staggered at different heights and x-positions across the basket's width.

For the baguette, I'm using a rotated capsule shape laid diagonally across the top of the basket, and considering adding a few small darker boxes as score marks on its surface, though keeping the orientation consistent with the baguette is tricky without merging geometries.

For the saddle, I'm scaling a sphere into a flattened leather seat shape, positioning it above the seat post, and planning small torus rings as springs to connect the saddle to the frame in classic Dutch bike style.

Now I'm laying out the main frame tubes -- seat tube, top tube, and down tube -- as swept geometries connecting the bottom bracket, seat tube top, and head tube junctions to form the bike's basic triangle structure.

I'm also planning the bone hierarchy: a root frame joint, with wheelF and wheelR joints for the wheels, and a steer joint at the head tube top that will parent the fork, handlebar, basket, bell, and flower decorations, keeping everything rigid since no rotation rigging is needed.

Now I'm checking ground clearance — the wheel's outer radius plus tube thickness means the hub needs to sit around y=0.36 so the tire bottom just touches y=0, and I'm recalculating the bottom bracket and other frame heights relative to that corrected hub position.

Working through the frame geometry, I'm placing the seat tube top, head tube top/bottom, top tube, down tube, seat stays, and chain stays, computing each endpoint from the bottom bracket and hub positions with reasonable real-world bike angles and offsets.

I'm positioning the steer tube joint, stem, and a tall riser handlebar arcing up and back with mirrored endpoints, then adding grips at the bar ends and placing a bell on the left side near the bar's bend.

For the bell, I'm using a hemisphere shape (flat side down) sized and positioned so its bottom touches the handlebar top, choosing silver as the color and skipping a bracket for simplicity. Now I'm figuring out where to place the front basket, aligning its depth and height relative to the handlebar stem, fender, and wheel so it sits naturally in front without overlapping other parts.

I'm working out dimensions and mount points for the basket, planning two chrome support sweeps from the steering area down to the basket corners, then sizing a tapered square frustum shape for the basket body and calculating how rotating it 45 degrees affects its final width and depth.

I'll position the basket centered around (0, 0.94, 0.70), with the bottom at 0.84 and top at 0.04 up to 1.04, giving it that tapered wicker look with the wider rim at top. I'm building each sunflower from a back disk, a petal ring, and a brown center disk layered slightly apart in depth, and adding a diagonal baguette resting on top of the basket rim so it pokes out front and back.

For the wheels, I'm constructing tires as tori with whitewall rings offset to the sides, silver hub cylinders, and sixteen alternating spokes per wheel radiating outward, giving roughly forty parts per wheel plus the frame. I'm adding curved fender bands using partial cylinders with specific theta ranges to wrap over the top of each wheel, plus a chain guard band positioned to cover the top and rear of the drivetrain area.

I'm placing the chainring and rear sprocket as thin cylinders on the x-axis, connecting them with swept chain lines along the top and bottom paths, and adding crank arms extending from the bottom bracket down to pedal boxes on each side. I'm finalizing the full color palette—mint, chrome, cream, tire black, basket tans, sunflower yellows and browns, and chain charcoal—landing around fourteen distinct flat colors, and confirming I'll use the sweep function with color options for all the curved parts before writing the actual part-generation code.

I'm defining joints for the frame, front and rear wheels, and steering column with specific positions, then building out mirrored pairs of frame tubes—seat tube, top tube, down tube, head tube, seat stays, chain stays, and fork blades—using a helper that mirrors coordinates across the x-axis for symmetry. I'm adding the seat post, saddle, springs, chain guard, bell as a hemisphere, and handlebar as a swept path, double-checking that geometry constructor arguments match Three.js conventions before writing the full wheel-building function with its spoke loop.
